nodes.label: Mongols sack Baghdad
nodes.full: Hulagu’s army destroys the Abbasid caliphate’s seat in 1258 and pushes into Syria — the vacuum and the threat this folio’s first forty years respond to.

nodes.label: The Black Death arrives
nodes.full: Plague reaches Alexandria by ship in 1347, on the same pandemic wave that is simultaneously striking Europe — a genuinely external, non-Mamluk event that this folio experiences rather than causes.

nodes.label: Timur invades Syria
nodes.full: The Central Asian conqueror Timur, having already broken the Delhi Sultanate and the Golden Horde, turns on Mamluk Syria in 1400 — a shock arriving from entirely outside the sultanate’s own political world.

nodes.label: Timur crushes the Golden Horde
nodes.full: Corrected on review — this node originally read "Ottomans close the Bosphorus" (c.1380), but the Ottomans did not command the straits that early. The better-supported driver: Timur’s wars against Khan Tokhtamysh (1391, then 1395–96) devastated the Qipchaq steppe’s cities and trade networks a few years before Barquq’s regime, disrupting the old recruitment pipeline and pushing it south to the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Ayalon (1949); correction added on review, not in the folio

nodes.label: The Ottoman gunpowder army matures
nodes.full: By the 1510s the Ottoman military had combined janissary infantry, massed arquebuses and chained field artillery into a doctrine no Mamluk-era cavalry army had had to face at this scale before.
nodes.src: Ayalon, "Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom" (1956)

nodes.label: Vasco da Gama rounds the Cape
nodes.full: Portugal’s direct sea route to the pepper coast of India, opened in 1498, is the external event that eventually breaks the Red Sea–Alexandria monopoly the Mamluk treasury had depended on since the Fatimids.

nodes.label: Constantinople falls to the Ottomans
nodes.full: Added on review — absent from the folio’s 89 entries. Mehmed II’s conquest gives the Ottomans full command of the Bosphorus and the Black Sea, turning a regional frontier power into the dominant Muslim state the Mamluks would eventually have to face directly.

nodes.label: Chaldiran — Selim turns south
nodes.full: Added on review — absent from the folio’s 89 entries. Selim I’s victory over Safavid Iran at Chaldiran frees his army from the eastern front, and Ottoman suspicion of contact between Cairo and Shah Ismail is cited as a further trigger — a specific reason the invasion came in 1516 and not another year.
nodes.src: Har-El (1995); background, not in the folio

nodes.label: Aybak & Shajar al-Durr
nodes.full: The Bahriyya regiment that murdered the last Ayyubid, Turanshah, put his widow Shajar al-Durr on the throne for eighty days, then married her to the atabeg Aybak. Aybak killed the Bahri leader Aqtay in 1254, driving Baybars into exile; in 1257 Shajar al-Durr had Aybak killed, and was herself beaten to death days later.

nodes.label: Qutuz — road to Ayn Jalut
nodes.full: As the Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus, the vice-sultan Qutuz deposed Aybak’s young son, recalled the exiled Bahris, and marched into Palestine. On the march home after Ayn Jalut, Baybars assassinated Qutuz and was acclaimed sultan in his place.

nodes.label: Baybars founds the state
nodes.full: Baybars built the institution: installed a refugee Abbasid as caliph for legitimacy, rebuilt the army and fleet, revived the relay post and signal system, and appointed a chief qadi for each of the four Sunni schools. He campaigned almost every year and allied with the Golden Horde against the Ilkhanate.

nodes.label: Qalawun’s succession
nodes.full: Baybars’ two sons were pushed aside within two years by the senior emir Qalawun, who founded the line that held the sultanate, on and off, for a century. He beat a full Ilkhanid invasion at Homs (1281) and built the great madrasa-hospital-mausoleum complex on Cairo’s main avenue.

nodes.label: Khalil takes Acre
nodes.full: Qalawun’s son completed the reduction of the crusader states: Acre stormed in May 1291, Tyre/Sidon/Beirut/Athlit abandoned within weeks. Two centuries of Latin rule on the Syrian mainland were over. He was assassinated by his own emirs in 1293.

nodes.label: al-Nasir Muhammad
nodes.full: Enthroned at nine and twice deposed by strongmen, al-Nasir Muhammad returned in 1310 to rule for thirty years: the 1323 peace, a vast building programme, the 1315 cadastral survey, and a court of splendour funded by ever-heavier extraction.
nodes.src: Levanoni (1995): his patronage undermined the system

nodes.label: The strongmen interregnum
nodes.full: In the gaps between al-Nasir Muhammad’s reigns the throne was held by Kitbugha (deposed amid famine), Lajin (murdered by his own mamluks), and the Circassian Baybars al-Jashnakir, whose brief rule (1309–10) foreshadowed the later regime.

nodes.label: Twelve sultans, forty-one years
nodes.full: Twelve members of al-Nasir’s family held the throne in 41 years, most installed and removed by rival emir factions; real power lay with magnates like Yalbugha al-Umari. The Black Death struck in the middle of it. Barquq set aside the last Qalawunid in 1382.

nodes.label: Barquq’s Circassian regime
nodes.full: A Circassian magnate risen through the Citadel-tower regiment, Barquq deposed the last Qalawunid and re-established a sultanate now recruited overwhelmingly from the Caucasus rather than the Qipchaq steppe. He faced down Timur’s first demands.
nodes.src: Ayalon, "The Circassians in the Mamluk Kingdom" (1949)

nodes.label: Faraj & the storm of Timur
nodes.full: Barquq’s teenage son inherited a war among the emirs and the onslaught of Timur, who sacked Aleppo and Damascus in 1400–1401. Faraj campaigned repeatedly against rebel viceroys and was finally caught and executed at Damascus in 1412.

nodes.label: Barsbay’s monopolies
nodes.full: Barsbay seized Cyprus in 1426, capturing King Janus, and forced the spice and sugar trades through crown monopolies at fixed prices — filling the treasury for a decade at the cost of the Karimi merchants and the transit economy’s long-term health.

nodes.label: Jaqmaq, Inal, Khushqadam
nodes.full: A run of elderly emirs elected by their peers: Jaqmaq raided Hospitaller Rhodes; Inal’s reign saw "the first serious Mamluk-Ottoman friction over the Karamanids." Government was by consensus among the great emirs, the treasury chronically short.

nodes.label: Qaytbay, the last strong sultan
nodes.full: A 29-year reign of relative stability: a long, costly, inconclusive war with the Ottomans (1485–91), and the last great flowering of Mamluk architecture — his madrasa, his Northern Cemetery complex. He left the treasury exhausted.

nodes.label: al-Ghawri, Tuman Bay, the end
nodes.full: Qansuh al-Ghawri rebuilt the Citadel’s defences and raised a corps of gunners, but marched north in 1516 with an army that still fought as horse-archers and died at Marj Dabiq. His nephew Tuman Bay held Cairo for months, lost at al-Raydaniyya, and was hanged at the Bab Zuwayla.

nodes.label: Ayn Jalut
nodes.full: The Mongol army left to hold Syria after Hulagu withdrew east was destroyed by Qutuz and Baybars in September 1260 — the first decisive defeat of a Mongol field force in open battle, fixing the Euphrates as the western limit of Mongol power.

nodes.label: The Ilkhanid invasions
nodes.full: Three more Ilkhanid attempts on Syria: beaten at Homs (1281); a Mamluk disaster at Wadi al-Khazandar (1299) that let Ghazan hold Damascus for a hundred days; the decisive Mamluk win at Shaqhab (1303). The frontier war ended with the formal peace of 1323.

nodes.label: Baybars breaks the Franks
nodes.full: A methodical sequence of sieges: Caesarea and Arsuf (1265), Safed (1266), the sack of Antioch (1268, the bloodiest single event of the crusading era), and in 1271 the Krak des Chevaliers.
nodes.src: Ibn Abd al-Zahir; the "Gestes des Chiprois"

nodes.label: The fall of Acre
nodes.full: Al-Ashraf Khalil stormed Acre in May 1291; the surviving Franks evacuated within weeks. Two centuries of Latin rule ended, and the Mamluks razed the coastal cities to deny them to any future crusade.

nodes.label: Nubia, Armenia, the Assassins
nodes.full: Baybars extended Mamluk reach in every direction: the Nizari Ismaili castles surrendered by 1273; Cilician Armenia was ravaged; a Mamluk army took Dongola in 1276, beginning the subjection of Christian Nubia.

nodes.label: The magnate households’ wars
nodes.full: With the Qalawunid sultans figureheads, real power was fought over by rival emir households — Yalbugha al-Umari, then Barquq’s rise, then the 1389–90 revolt that briefly unseated him.

nodes.label: Timur sacks Aleppo & Damascus
nodes.full: Timur crushed the Mamluk garrisons of northern Syria and took Damascus after a siege during which Ibn Khaldun was lowered over the wall to negotiate. The Umayyad Mosque burned; Damascus’s craftsmen were deported to Samarqand.

nodes.label: The conquest of Cyprus
nodes.full: In reprisal for piracy and a raid that burned part of the Nile Delta, Barsbay’s fleets routed the Lusignan army and captured King Janus — a rare Mamluk conquest overseas.

nodes.label: Taurus frontier war
nodes.full: Six years of fighting over the buffer principality of Dulkadir; Qaytbay’s general Azbak held his ground and the war closed in a status-quo peace — the last time the Mamluks fought the Ottomans to a draw.

nodes.label: Chaul and Diu
nodes.full: A Mamluk fleet allied with Gujarat beat a Portuguese squadron at Chaul in 1508; the next year it was annihilated off Diu. The Indian Ocean, and the spice route, passed to Portugal.

nodes.label: Marj Dabiq
nodes.full: North of Aleppo, Selim I’s janissary infantry with arquebuses behind chained field guns broke the Mamluk cavalry charge. Al-Ghawri died on the field as Khayrbak, the viceroy of Aleppo, defected. All of Syria fell within weeks.

nodes.label: al-Raydaniyya & Cairo’s fall
nodes.full: Tuman Bay dug in with hastily cast cannon north of Cairo; the Ottomans turned his flank and took the city after days of street fighting. Selim had him hanged at the Bab Zuwayla.

nodes.label: A one-generation caste
nodes.full: Political power was reserved to men bought as boys on the Qipchaq steppe or in the Caucasus, converted, trained, and manumitted. Their own sons, the awlad al-nas, were barred from the elite — a deliberately non-hereditary state that renewed itself by import every generation.

nodes.label: The Abbasid shadow caliph
nodes.full: Baybars had a fugitive Abbasid uncle acclaimed as caliph, and thereafter each sultan took investiture from a powerless Abbasid at the Citadel — a fig-leaf of legitimacy for 256 years, until Selim I carried the last one to Istanbul.

nodes.label: The four chief qadis
nodes.full: Baybars replaced the single Shafi’i chief judge with one chief qadi for each of the four Sunni law schools, giving all four equal standing — a reform that spread through the Sunni world.

nodes.label: The iqta & the 1315 survey
nodes.full: The military land-assignment system reached its most elaborate form under the Qalawunids: al-Nasir Muhammad’s 1315 survey (al-rawk al-Nasiri) redistributed Egypt’s revenue and cut the halqa’s share.

nodes.label: The 1301 anti-dhimmi edict
nodes.full: Pressed by jurists and mobs, al-Nasir Muhammad’s government issued the harshest anti-dhimmi measures of medieval Egypt: officials dismissed, churches closed, dress rules enforced, repeated in 1321 and 1354.

nodes.label: Government by military office
nodes.full: The state ran through a hierarchy of military-rank offices — viceroy, commander-in-chief, executive secretary, household steward — held by emirs, with a civilian scribal bureaucracy under them.

nodes.label: Servant of the Two Sanctuaries
nodes.full: The sultan appointed the Sharifs of Mecca, sent the kiswa and grain for the Hijaz, and dispatched the pilgrim caravan with the mahmal — making Cairo, not Baghdad, the working centre of Sunni Islam.

nodes.label: Twin capitals of Sunni learning
nodes.full: With Baghdad destroyed, the Mamluk cities became the centre of gravity of Sunni scholarship — hundreds of endowed madrasas, a dense network of teaching licences drawing students from the Maghreb to India.

nodes.label: Ibn Taymiyya
nodes.full: The Damascus Hanbali jurist campaigned against saint-cults and speculative theology, and issued fatwas declaring jihad against the nominally-Muslim Ilkhanids licit. Tried and imprisoned repeatedly, he died in the Damascus citadel in 1328.

nodes.label: The tariqas & the age of the saint
nodes.full: Organised Sufism pervaded society: the Shadhiliyya, the Rifaiyya and Qadiriyya, and the cult of Ahmad al-Badawi of Tanta, whose mawlid remains Egypt’s largest religious festival.

nodes.label: Ibn Arabi’s school
nodes.full: Ibn Arabi’s metaphysics of the unity of being was carried into the mainstream by al-Qunawi, al-Qashani and al-Jili — and drew sustained attack from Ibn Taymiyya and others.

nodes.label: The age of hadith scholarship
nodes.full: The Mamluk schools produced the standing apparatus of Sunni hadith study — al-Mizzi, al-Dhahabi, and above all Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani’s "Fath al-Bari", never superseded.

nodes.label: The Copts retreat to the desert
nodes.full: Under fiscal pressure, mob violence and the 1301 edicts, the Coptic community contracted sharply — its centre of gravity moving to the desert monasteries of Wadi Natrun.

nodes.label: The Jewish nagid
nodes.full: The Rabbanite and Karaite communities shrank with the general population and anti-dhimmi pressure, but kept their institutions; the nagid was often a Maimonidean descendant.

nodes.label: Quranic recitation systematised
nodes.full: Ibn al-Jazari of Damascus fixed the science of Quranic recitation; his works on the ten canonical readings remain the standard reference.

nodes.label: The stone city of the Mamluks
nodes.full: The Mamluk emirs competed in stone: Qalawun’s madrasa-hospital-mausoleum, the colossal madrasa-mosque of Sultan Hasan, hundreds of smaller complexes each with a domed founder’s tomb.

nodes.label: The carved domes of the Circassians
nodes.full: Cairo’s masons cut complex geometric and floral patterns into stone dome exteriors, culminating in Qaytbay’s Northern Cemetery complex — often called the most perfectly resolved Mamluk building.

nodes.label: Inlaid metalwork & the blazon
nodes.full: Brass basins and boxes inlaid with silver and gold, covered in blazons — the cup-bearer’s cup, the secretary’s pen-box. The "Baptistere de Saint Louis" is the masterpiece; lighter export versions reached Venice.

nodes.label: Enamelled glass, and its end
nodes.full: Syrian enamelled glass reached its height in the great mosque lamps — then died abruptly when Timur deported the Damascus glassmakers to Samarqand in 1401.

nodes.label: The monumental Quran
nodes.full: Sultans endowed their madrasas with huge multi-volume Qurans in bold muhaqqaq script; the Cairo and Damascus ateliers set a standard later Ilkhanid and Timurid patrons imitated.

nodes.label: Encyclopedias & the chancery arts
nodes.full: The age’s characteristic form was the vast compilation: al-Nuwayri’s "Nihayat al-Arab", al-Qalqashandi’s "Subh al-Asha", and al-Safadi’s biographical dictionaries.

nodes.label: Shadow theatre & the Nights
nodes.full: Ibn Daniyal wrote the only surviving medieval Arabic drama texts; the "Sirat Baybars" epic took shape around the Mamluk founder; the "Thousand and One Nights" reached its familiar form in Mamluk Syria.

nodes.label: Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddima
nodes.full: The Tunisian jurist-historian settled in Mamluk Cairo in 1382 and completed the "Muqaddima" — his theory of asabiyya and the cyclical rise and decay of dynasties. In 1401 he was lowered over Damascus’s wall to meet Timur.

nodes.label: The Egyptian school of historians
nodes.full: A continuous, self-aware tradition of urban history: al-Maqrizi’s "al-Khitat" and "al-Suluk", Ibn Taghribirdi’s "al-Nujum al-Zahira", and Ibn Iyas, an eyewitness to the Ottoman conquest.

nodes.label: Ibn al-Nafis & the lungs
nodes.full: The physician argued that blood passes right-to-left through the lungs, not invisible septal pores — the pulmonary circulation, three centuries before Servetus. He was chief physician of the Mansuri hospital.

nodes.label: Ibn al-Shatir’s astronomy
nodes.full: The Umayyad Mosque’s timekeeper built planetary models eliminating the Ptolemaic equant — mathematically identical to those Copernicus published in 1543.

nodes.label: The muwaqqit’s mathematics
nodes.full: Mamluk mosques employed salaried astronomers to fix prayer times and the qibla; al-Khalili’s Damascus tables sustained a genuine applied-mathematics research programme.

nodes.label: The Lisan al-Arab & the Qamus
nodes.full: Two of the largest Arabic dictionaries ever compiled: Ibn Manzur’s twenty-volume "Lisan al-Arab" and al-Fayruzabadi’s "al-Qamus al-Muhit", the desk reference for five centuries.

nodes.label: The plague treatises
nodes.full: The Black Death forced scholars to debate contagion versus divine visitation and whether flight was permitted. Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti both wrote plague tracts.

nodes.label: The Karimi transit trade
nodes.full: Egypt monopolised the flow of pepper and spices from the Indian Ocean through Aden and the Red Sea to Alexandria; the Karimi — some fifty great families — financed it and banked the sultans.

nodes.label: Barsbay’s monopolies
nodes.full: Barsbay forced sugar then pepper through crown monopolies at fixed prices — filling the treasury for a decade and destroying the Karimi as an independent force.

nodes.label: The Black Death, economically
nodes.full: The first wave killed perhaps a third of Egypt and Syria; the state — dependent on a centrally managed irrigation system — recovered less than western Europe did.

nodes.label: The copper inflation
nodes.full: The silver dirham vanished; the state flooded the market with copper fulus. Al-Maqrizi’s "Ighathat al-Umma" blames monetary mismanagement, corruption, and the plague.

nodes.label: The slave-trade supply chain
nodes.full: Qipchaq Turks shipped through Genoese Caffa and the Bosphorus fed the Bahri army; as the Ottomans closed the straits, Circassians brought overland from the Caucasus took over — the Suq al-Nakhkhasin in Cairo was the clearing house.

nodes.label: The Venetian & Genoese factories
nodes.full: Venice, Genoa and Catalonia kept fortified compounds at Alexandria and Damascus; Egypt sent cotton, spices and sugar out against silver, wool and metal.

nodes.label: The rural crisis
nodes.full: After the plague, cultivated area contracted; emirs milked their iqtas for cash, the irrigation corvee broke down, and Bedouin tribes moved into the vacuum.

nodes.label: The Portuguese spice collapse
nodes.full: Vasco da Gama’s Cape route let Portugal sell pepper below the Alexandria price. Venetian purchases fell by more than half — "a fiscal wound the Ottoman conquest merely finished."

nodes.label: Resisting the hand-gun
nodes.full: The Mamluks used siege cannon but the cavalry corps despised the hand-gun as unfit for a horseman. Al-Ghawri’s late arquebus corps came far too late to answer Ottoman firepower at Marj Dabiq.

nodes.label: Furusiyya
nodes.full: Mamluk training was codified in a large technical literature on riding, lance and mounted archery, practised in the hippodromes below the Citadel — a military system and the ruling caste’s cultural core.

nodes.label: Relay post & pigeon service
nodes.full: Baybars rebuilt a state relay-post to the Euphrates, a pigeon service with registered pedigrees, and fire-and-smoke towers that could warn Cairo of a Mongol crossing within a day.

nodes.label: Block-printed amulets
nodes.full: Craftsmen printed miniature Quranic texts from carved blocks onto paper amulets — a working block-printing technology two centuries before Gutenberg, confined to charms.

nodes.label: Sugar & saltpetre
nodes.full: The Egyptian sugar industry ran mechanised presses and refining houses; the same base supported saltpetre for gunpowder. The sugar works decayed with the rural economy after 1400.

nodes.label: The Golden Horde alliance
nodes.full: Baybars allied with Berke, the first Muslim Golden Horde khan, against the Ilkhanate; the alliance kept open the Black Sea route that supplied Mamluk slave-recruits.

nodes.label: Peace with the Mongols
nodes.full: After sixty years of frontier war, al-Nasir Muhammad and the Ilkhan Abu Said signed a formal peace — the Ilkhanate had by then converted to Islam.

nodes.label: Diplomacy replaces the Crusades
nodes.full: With Outremer gone, the Mamluks dealt with Latin Christendom through treaties covering trade, piracy, ransom, and pilgrim access to Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Ibn Battuta passes through
nodes.full: The Tangier traveller crossed Alexandria, Cairo, Damascus and the Hijaz; his "Rihla" is one of the fullest descriptions of Mamluk cities at their height.

nodes.label: Mansa Musa’s hajj
nodes.full: The ruler of Mali crossed Egypt on pilgrimage with so much gold that the Cairo gold price had not recovered a decade later.

nodes.label: Embassies from Ming China
nodes.full: As protector of Mecca the sultan received missions from Gujarat, Bengal, Vijayanagara and Ceylon, and via Aden from Zheng He’s Ming treasure fleets.

nodes.label: European eyes on Egypt
nodes.full: Latin pilgrims, consuls and crusade-recovery authors like Marino Sanudo left accounts that shaped how Europe pictured the Mamluk state.

nodes.label: The Mongols are stopped
nodes.full: Ayn Jalut and the sixty-year defence of the Euphrates preserved a major independent Islamic power in the west exactly as the eastern Islamic world fell under Mongol rule.

nodes.label: The Latin East is liquidated
nodes.full: The fall of Acre ended the crusader states; never again a Latin territorial foothold on the Syrian mainland.

nodes.label: Cairo, greatest city west of China
nodes.full: With Baghdad in ruins, Mamluk Cairo — perhaps half a million people before the plague — was the largest city in the Mediterranean world.

nodes.label: The Black Death, as world event
nodes.full: Plague swept Egypt and Syria in 1347–49; the state’s dependence on centralised irrigation meant lasting structural damage western Europe’s decentralised agriculture escaped.

nodes.label: The spice route rounds Africa
nodes.full: The Cape route broke the monopoly underwriting Egyptian state finance since the Fatimids; the naval counter-effort failed at Diu, and customs revenue collapsed on the eve of conquest.

nodes.label: End of medieval Egypt
nodes.full: Selim I’s victories made Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz Ottoman provinces and carried the last Cairo Abbasid to Istanbul. A native regime would not rule Cairo again until the 20th century.

nodes.label: Cavalry state vs gunpowder empire
nodes.full: The textbook case of a mounted-warrior state overrun by a gunpowder empire — how much was technology and how much the defections of Khayrbak and Janbirdi al-Ghazali is still argued.

nodes.label: The making of a Mamluk
nodes.full: A boy of eight to twelve, bought on the steppe or in the Caucasus, was shipped to Cairo, housed in the barracks, converted, taught horsemanship, and manumitted — bound for life to his master and cohort.

nodes.label: The great ladies of the Citadel
nodes.full: From Shajar al-Durr onward, the khawand controlled fortunes, founded mosques and madrasas, and occasionally ran the government behind a child sultan.

nodes.label: The awlad al-nas
nodes.full: The children of Mamluks, born free, were barred from the military elite their fathers held — becoming instead the scholars, historians and bureaucrats of Mamluk society.

nodes.label: The eunuchs of the Citadel
nodes.full: Eunuchs, enslaved and castrated outside the empire, tutored the boy-Mamluks, guarded the harem and treasury, and kept the Prophet’s mosque in Medina.

nodes.label: The beloved in Mamluk letters
nodes.full: Biographical dictionaries are full of the love of men for beautiful youths — al-Safadi wrote both verse and a treatise on it — set against the jurists’ flat prohibition.

nodes.label: Plague at eye level
nodes.full: Al-Maqrizi records the biers backed up at the mosques, whole streets of Cairo emptied, the soaring price of a gravedigger’s spade.

nodes.label: Household slavery’s hierarchy
nodes.full: Below the military slaves, far more numerous household slaves were ranked by origin — Turkish and Circassian at the top, sub-Saharan African at the bottom doing the heaviest work.
